records.digest: Every country should run newborn screening for PKU. Finding babies early is what makes early treatment possible, and it pays for itself.
records.nc_note: North Carolina requires a blood spot on every baby born in the state under G.S. 130A-125, and PKU has been screened here since 1966.

records.digest: Test mothers who were never screened themselves, especially if their baby shows high phenylalanine or signs of maternal PKU syndrome.
records.nc_note: US centers do test the mother when an infant screens positive or presents with the maternal PKU pattern, so the reactive half happens.

records.digest: Before starting treatment, rule out BH4 cofactor defects and DNAJC12 deficiency, which look similar but need different treatment.
records.nc_note: DNAJC12 testing is not routine anywhere in the US and usually turns up only through a broader gene panel or exome, so that step is inconsistent here.

records.digest: Genotype the patient. It separates PAH deficiency from lookalikes, hints at sapropterin response, and helps pin down severity.
records.nc_note: The 2024 ACMG guideline goes further than Europe and recommends PAH genetic testing at birth for every confirmed case.

records.digest: Sort patients into groups: no treatment needed below 360, treatment needed and cofactor responsive, or treatment needed and not responsive.
records.nc_note: The practical dividing line is the same, because ACMG also puts the treatment threshold at 360 umol/L, but the vocabulary a North Carolina family hears in clinic is not the European scheme.

records.digest: Begin treatment as fast as possible, ideally before the baby is ten days old.
records.nc_note: US guidance also calls for treatment in the first week to ten days of life, and North Carolina screens early enough to permit that.

records.digest: Do not treat below 360. Keep checking at low frequency until at least age six in case levels climb.

records.digest: Start treatment in any child whose untreated level reaches 360 or above.

records.digest: Through age twelve, aim to keep blood phenylalanine between 120 and 360.

records.digest: Everyone with PKU needs lifelong follow-up at a specialist metabolic centre, including adults not taking any phenylalanine-lowering treatment.
records.nc_note: The US loses most adults. Published estimates put more than half of all US patients outside metabolic clinic care, and roughly 71 percent of adults aged 19 to 45 not actively treated.

records.digest: Provide at least 200 mg a day of DHA before and during pregnancy.
records.nc_note: There is no US requirement that prenatal vitamins contain DHA and no coverage guarantee for DHA supplements, so a North Carolina woman buys it herself.

records.digest: Measure folate, vitamin B12, MCV and ferritin, full blood count, and plasma amino acids before conception and in early pregnancy.
records.nc_note: US metabolic clinics order this panel and plasma amino acids at a specialty lab, so it happens for enrolled patients.

records.digest: Support breastfeeding after a PKU pregnancy, whether or not the baby has PKU.
records.nc_note: US law requires most plans to cover lactation support and a pump, and North Carolina newborn screening catches an affected infant fast, so the clinical setup is decent.

records.digest: Keep up attentive postpartum care, with practical and nutritional support through lactation whichever treatment path she chooses.
records.nc_note: North Carolina Medicaid's 12 month postpartum extension keeps her insured, which is the strongest piece of the US answer here.

records.digest: Provide education and emotional support before and during pregnancy, and bring partners and family in so they can help.
records.nc_note: In the US this education is done by clinic dietitians and by patient organizations like NPKUA, not by any funded program, and it only reaches women already connected to one of them.

records.digest: Test for PKU in any unscreened child or adult with intellectual disability or neurological problems, with or without psychiatric symptoms.
records.nc_note: North Carolina has screened every newborn for PKU since 1966, so a US-born adult is rarely missed and this recommendation mostly bites for immigrants and refugees.

records.nc_note: Roughly 71 percent of US adults with PKU are not in a metabolic clinic at all, which means most of them cannot reach any of these options.

records.digest: Consider sapropterin responsiveness for every PAH-deficient patient except those with two known null variants.
records.nc_note: North Carolina also has an option this guideline does not address, sepiapterin (Sephience), FDA approved July 28, 2025 for ages one month and up at a wholesale cost near $480,000 per year.

records.digest: Run a formal response test, measuring how blood phenylalanine changes after a sapropterin dose, to find who benefits.
records.nc_note: US clinics follow the ACMG protocol, a 10 to 20 mg/kg daily trial running up to one month, not the European short loading test, so a North Carolina newborn may start diet before responsiveness is known.

records.digest: Prove long-term response in a trial that adjusts dose, natural protein, and substitute. Benefit means natural protein tolerance at least doubles.
records.nc_note: North Carolina plans renew sapropterin on a 30 percent blood Phe reduction from baseline, not on doubled natural protein tolerance, so the European benefit measure is not the one being scored.

records.digest: Patients on sapropterin get the same clinical, biochemical, and nutritional follow-up as everyone else with PKU.
records.nc_note: Physician visits and lab draws bill to insurance in North Carolina, but metabolic dietitian time is poorly reimbursed and the state runs on a small number of metabolic centers, mainly UNC Chapel Hill and Duke.

records.digest: Review diet, micronutrients, and nutritional bloodwork annually, especially in anyone who has cut back or stopped protein substitute.
records.nc_note: NC Medicaid covers metabolic formula at any age when the metabolic disorder was diagnosed before age 10, but North Carolina has no state medical food mandate for commercial plans, and self-funded employer plans are exempt from state mandates regardless.

records.digest: Sapropterin response testing may be considered before conception, particularly where diet alone has not reached target levels.
records.nc_note: The US sapropterin label carries no pregnancy contraindication and the PKUDOS and KAMPER registries support continued use, so a North Carolina responder can usually stay on it through pregnancy.

records.digest: Patients over sixteen who cannot reach control on sapropterin may be offered pegvaliase, with close follow-up given its safety profile.
records.nc_note: The FDA label now reaches age 12, younger than the European floor of 16, but North Carolina payer criteria commonly still require age 18 and a blood Phe above 600 micromol/L on existing management, which locks out patients sitting between 360 and 600.

records.digest: The aim with pegvaliase is a safe protein intake of at least 0.8 g/kg/day without protein substitute, or lower blood phenylalanine.
records.nc_note: A North Carolina patient can have a Palynziq prescription worth roughly $130,000 to $443,000 per year approved as a specialty drug while paying cash for the low protein bread and pasta that make an ordinary 0.8 g/kg protein intake livable.
